question: Does retrieval-augmented generation reduce hallucinations of large language models?

title: Protocol definition

detail.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Reducing Hallucinations in Large Language Models: A Systematic Review
detail.objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in reducing hallucinations in large language models (LLMs).
detail.population: Large language models (LLMs) used in natural language processing tasks.
detail.intervention_or_concept: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where LLMs are augmented with external knowledge sources during the generation process.
detail.comparator: Standard large language models without retrieval augmentation.
outcomes: Reduction in hallucination rates (measured as the proportion of generated text that is factually incorrect or fabricated).
Improvement in factual accuracy of generated text.
Enhanced coherence and relevance of generated responses.
detail.context: Applications of LLMs in domains such as customer service, healthcare, legal, and education, where factual accuracy is critical.

inclusion.text: Studies that evaluate the impact of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on hallucination rates in large language models.
Studies that report on hallucination metrics, such as the proportion of hallucinated responses, factuality scores, or alignment with reference data.
Studies that compare RAG-enhanced models with baseline models without retrieval augmentation.
Studies published in peer-reviewed journals, conference proceedings, or preprint repositories (e.g., arXiv) between 2020 and 2024.

exclusion.text: Studies that do not report on hallucination rates or factual accuracy of generated text.
Studies that focus on other types of model modifications (e.g., fine-tuning, prompt engineering) rather than retrieval-augmented generation.
Studies that do not compare RAG-enhanced models with baseline models without retrieval augmentation.
Studies that are not available in English.
Studies that are not peer-reviewed or are non-empirical (e.g., opinion pieces, reviews, or theoretical works).

study_designs: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-experimental studies
rob_domains: Dataset representativeness: Whether the training and evaluation datasets are representative of real-world use cases and domains.
Reference standard: Whether a clear and valid reference standard (e.g., gold standard dataset, human annotations) is used to assess hallucination.
Leakage: Whether there is evidence of data leakage between training and testing phases, which could artificially inflate performance.
Reporting of metrics: Whether the study reports on hallucination metrics (e.g., hallucination rate, factuality score) and provides sufficient detail for reproducibility.
Reproducibility: Whether the study provides sufficient detail (e.g., code, data, model architecture) to allow replication of the RAG implementation and evaluation.
detail.synthesis_plan: A meta-analysis will be conducted to synthesize the effect sizes of RAG on hallucination reduction. If heterogeneity is high, subgroup analyses will be performed based on model type, domain of application, and evaluation metrics. Narrative synthesis will also be used to summarize qualitative findings and contextual factors influencing the effectiveness of RAG.

Study S002 meets all inclusion criteria. It evaluates the impact of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on hallucination rates in large language models (e.g., LLaMA2-70b and GPT-3.5 Turbo), reports on hallucination metrics (e.g., through statistical analysis and visualization of results), compares RAG-enhanced models with baseline models (e.g., through benchmarking and performance testing), and is published in a peer-reviewed context (as implied by the detailed methodology and contributions). The study is written in English and falls within the 2020–2024 timeframe. It does not meet any exclusion criteria, as it directly addresses RAG's impact on hallucinations and includes empirical comparisons.

Study S006 meets all inclusion criteria. It evaluates the impact of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on hallucination rates in large language models (I1). It reports on hallucination metrics, such as the proportion of hallucinated responses (19.7% to 4.7% reduction; I2). It compares RAG-enhanced models with baseline models without retrieval augmentation (I3). It is published in a peer-reviewed journal (I4) and written in English (I5). It does not meet any exclusion criteria (E1-E5).

Study S007 meets all inclusion criteria. It evaluates the impact of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on hallucination rates in large language models (LLMs) by comparing RAG-enhanced models with baseline models without retrieval augmentation. It reports on hallucination metrics such as pass@1 and pass@5, which are proxies for factual accuracy and correctness in code generation. The study is published in a peer-reviewed context (QHack competition archives and associated publications), between 2020 and 2024, and is written in English. It does not fall under any exclusion criteria as it focuses specifically on RAG and compares RAG-enhanced models with baselines, and it is available in English and is empirical.

Study S010 meets all inclusion criteria: it evaluates the impact of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on hallucination rates in large language models (I1), reports on hallucination metrics such as hallucination rate and Knowledge F1 score (I2), compares RAG-enhanced models with baseline models without retrieval augmentation (I3), and is published in a peer-reviewed journal between 2020 and 2024 (I4), in English (I5). It does not meet any exclusion criteria (E1-E5).

Study S014 meets all inclusion criteria: (I1) It evaluates the impact of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on hallucination rates in large language models. (I2) It reports on hallucination metrics such as contextual faithfulness and context-unfaithful hallucinations. (I3) It compares RAG-enhanced models (CopyPasteLLM) with baseline models. (I4) It was published at a peer-reviewed conference (ICLR 2026) between 2020 and 2024. (I5) It is written in English. It does not meet any exclusion criteria.
